main_topic.h_title: Authentic Thai Massaman Curry with Chicken
main_topic.main_title: Authentic Thai Massaman Curry with Chicken
main_topic.author: Hot Thai Kitchen

primary_content.text: For many people, massaman is their favourite of all Thai curries because of the tender braised chicken, flavourful potatoes, and aromatic spices. It's so popular that it was once voted "the most delicious food in the world by a CNN poll! I'll show you a hack for making a quick semi-homemade massaman curry paste that will beat anything you can buy. I've been making massaman curry since I was a kid in Thailand, and I promise it'll beat anything you get at a restaurant!

main_topic.main_title: Authentic Thai Massaman Curry with Chicken
main_topic.author: Hot Thai Kitchen

primary_content.text: In the context of Thai cuisine, massaman curry is unique in that it is thicker and richer than others like green curry or red curry. It also uniquely uses a lot of dry spices such as cinnamon, cloves, and cumin, whereas other Thai curries rely mostly on fresh herbs. This makes the flavour of massaman more reminiscent of Indian curries. The use of potatoes, a vegetable otherwise quite rare in Thai cuisine, is also its identifying feature.

Massaman curry is believed to have come to Thailand via the south, from the Malay people who are Muslims. This is why in Thailand massaman curry is considered a Muslim-Thai food. Because of that, you will find massaman curries in Thailand made with chicken, beef, or even goat, but never pork, despite pork being the most popular meat in Thailand!

Massaman is typically a mild curry, so it is also one that's perfect starter curries for kids or for those with low spice tolerance. For another mild Thai curry that similarly has lots of dry spices, try Thai yellow curry.

main_topic.main_title: Authentic Thai Massaman Curry with Chicken
main_topic.author: Hot Thai Kitchen

primary_content.text: Here are all the ingredients you'll need for massaman and important notes about them. For amounts, check out the full recipe card below.

Bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs and/or drumsticks. Trim off excess fat from chicken thighs. If you want to substitute beef, check out this luxurious massaman beef short rubs recipe, or this Instant Pot massaman curry which uses chuck. Pork is not typically used for massaman curry because it is a dish of Muslim origin.

Massaman curry paste. If you can find premade massaman curry paste, you can use it, but I recommend you make a quick semi-homemade paste using store bought red curry paste as a base (recipe follows). It will be much better!
Palm sugar, or substitute light brown sugar or granulated sugar

Tamarind paste. Tamarind is added for a little acidity which helps balance the richness of the curry. You can use pre-made Thai tamarind paste (also labeled as tamarind concentrate) or make you own from pulp. If you're unfamiliar, read this article all about tamarind. If you can't find tamarind, a touch of Worcestershire sauce or vinegar will be fine in a pinch.
Bay leaves. Totally optional, throw them in if you've got some!

Potato. You can use any kind but it's best to avoid starchy varieties such as Russet as they fall apart easily when overcooked. I like Yukon Gold, an all-purpose potato, but waxy potatoes also work great. Some prefer sweet potato, but be sure to use yellow-flesh sweet potatoes and NOT orange yams which are too soft and watery.
Yellow or white onion, cut into 1 cm strips vertically.
Roasted whole peanuts. I prefer roasting my own from raw peanuts as the flavours are much fresher, but pre-roasted is fine in a pinch.

main_topic.main_title: Authentic Thai Massaman Curry with Chicken
main_topic.author: Hot Thai Kitchen

primary_content.text: If you can find a good brand of massaman curry paste—great, but if you have a little extra time, I recommend making this quick, semi-homemade version using store bought red curry paste as a base. I figured out this trick after realizing that massaman curry paste is basically red curry paste PLUS some spices, but commercial massaman pastes don't add much spices due to cost, so at home, we can make a version that's fully loaded and create a much more aromatic curry.
Green or white cardamom, in Thailand we use white cardamom, but green cardamom works just fine and they're much more widely available.
Coriander seeds
Cumin seeds
Ground cinnamon
Ground nutmeg, or freshly grated

Red curry paste, store bought. A good brand is important here. I recommend Maeploy, Aroy D, or Namjai. Thai Kitchen brand is not recommended unless you need a curry that is not spicy at all (for kids, perhaps), and you will want to use the whole jar for this recipe. You can also read about my Red Curry Paste Review for more about how I make these recommendations.

Fermented shrimp paste (optional). Thai fermented shrimp paste ( gapi) is a thick purplish brown paste that adds umami and depth to Thai curries. We add it to all curries in Thailand but it is often omitted from commercial pastes to make it vegan, so for the best flavour we gotta add it back in! Note: I add shrimp paste even if the curry paste already contains it to boost the umami.

secondary_content.text: *If you like to DIY you can also make homemade massaman curry paste from scratch.

main_topic.main_title: Authentic Thai Massaman Curry with Chicken
main_topic.author: Hot Thai Kitchen

primary_content.text: Most of my recipes come with a detailed video tutorial, and if this is your first time I highly recommend watching the video tutorial to ensure success!

main_topic.main_title: Authentic Thai Massaman Curry with Chicken
main_topic.author: Hot Thai Kitchen

primary_content.text: Here's a bird's eye view of the process. If this is your first time, I highly recommend watching the full video tutorial first to ensure success. For the full recipe with ingredient amounts, see the recipe card below.
For the semi-homemade massaman curry paste: Toast the cumin seeds over medium high heat, moving constantly, until the darken slightly. Remove from heat.
Toast all the other whole spices, moving them constantly, until the coriander seeds darken slightly. Remove from heat.
Grind the spices into a powder in a mortar and pestle or coffee grinder. Then add the ground cinnamon and nutmeg.
Add the shrimp paste and red curry paste and pound to mix. If using a coffee grinder, transfer to a mixing bowl and mix with a spoon.

Optional step: add a little oil to a heavy bottomed pot (the one you'll use to make the curry) and heat over medium high heat until hot. Sear the skin side of the chicken without moving for about 4 minutes until browned. Remove and repeat with the remaining chicken.
Pour off excess oil, then return the pot to the stove and about ½ cup of the coconut milk. Bring to a boil, scraping the bottom to release browned bits.
Add the curry paste and stir to mix, reduce heat to about medium.

Keep sauteing the paste for 3-4 minutes, until the oil starts to separate from the paste. If after 4 minutes the oil does not separate, you can move on; some coconut milk has been processed to prevent separation.
Add the remaining coconut milk and stir to mix. Add bay leaves (break/bruise them first), then add all of the palm sugar, half the fish sauce, and half the tamarind.
Add the chicken, along with any juices collected in the bowl. The chicken should be almost fully submerged; if not, add a little more water.
Partially cover the pot and bring to a gentle simmer. Simmer for 35 minutes.

After 35 minutes, the chicken should be almost tender but not quite there. Oil floating on the surface is the iconic look of massaman and there's no need to skim it, but if there's way too much oil for your taste, feel free to skim some off.

Add the potatoes, onions and half of the peanuts, and push the potatoes down so they are just barely submerged. If there's not enough liquid, add a little more water. Don't worry about submerging the onions as they will wilt down.
Simmer for 10-15 minutes until the potatoes can be pieced through with a fork easily. Turn off the heat.
Taste and add more fish sauce and/or tamarind paste as needed. Make it strongly seasoned as it will be served over rice. Garnish with more peanuts and enjoy!

main_topic.main_title: Authentic Thai Massaman Curry with Chicken
main_topic.author: Hot Thai Kitchen

primary_content.text: Massaman curry keeps very well. In fact, I recommend making it one day in advance for even better flavour. In the fridge, in an airtight container, the curry will keep for up to a week.

You can freeze massaman curry paste, and I recommend freezing in single portions so it's easy to use. Or you can also freeze the curry sauce to make dinner even faster - so cook the paste and add the coconut milk and seasonings, but don't add the meat and veggies. Then all you have to do is thaw the sauce and add meat and veg.

When you reheat, microwaving is fine, but take it out and give it a stir a couple of times in between. It'll also help if you break the chicken up into two smaller chunks. If reheating on the stovetop I would remove the potatoes as they might overcook and fall apart during the reheat. Add the potatoes back in in the last couple of minutes.

primary_content.text: If you're a fan of Thai curries, check out these other popular and equally easy recipes.

Red curry is what I consider the most basic of all curries so it's a good one to start, and just about any Asian market sells red curry paste! Here's a chicken red curry with squash, and a red pineapple curry with shrimp.
Yellow curry is something else to try if you want to stick to the stewy, rich curry similar to massaman. I have both yellow curry chicken and yellow curry with beef.

secondary_content.text: Green curry is a classic, and there's a really good vegan green curry, too!
